summary: Portugal is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, nationals of the countries and territories on the EU's visa-exempt list (Annex II of Regulation 2018/1806) can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorization is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (general fee €90). Long-stay options include residency visas for people living from passive income and for digital nomads working remotely.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

Portugal's visa portal says a Schengen visa holder should have or be able to legally obtain €75 for each entry and €40 for each day, or present a statement of responsibility signed by a national citizen or legal resident.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders: on the first crossing since the EES started, border officers take a facial photo and/or scan fingerprints. The EU says this can be quicker if you register some of your data in advance, at a self-service system or through a mobile app where one is available. The UK government's travel advice says there is no cost for EES registration.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Portugal travel advice: entry requirements

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The official EU site is travel-europe.europa.eu.

source.name: ETIAS — Official EU website

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

source.name: Your Europe (EU) — travelling with cash

notes: The EU's Your Europe portal says that when you arrive from outside the EU you can bring in, free of VAT and excise duty and not for resale, 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco), 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus 1 litre of spirits over 22% or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine, and other goods worth up to €300 (€430 if you travel by air or sea). Travellers under 17 get no tobacco or alcohol allowance.

The UK FCDO says you cannot take meat, milk or products containing them into EU countries, with some exceptions such as powdered baby milk, baby food and special foods or pet feed required for medical reasons.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office advises being alert to street crime: take care on public transport and at crowded bus and tram stops, where thieves use distraction techniques and often work in teams. Attacks, including sexual assaults, are rare but do occur, most often late at night around nightlife areas.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts stays across the whole Schengen Area, not only in Portugal.
The Government of Canada says pickpocketing and bag snatching are common in Lisbon and Porto, and advises extra caution on Lisbon's trams 15, 25 and 28.
The Government of Canada says most highways in Portugal require tolls, that you may need to pay electronically, and that international credit or debit cards are not always accepted.
The official ETIAS website, travel-europe.europa.eu, gives the fee as EUR 20 when you apply through it; applicants under 18 or over 70 are exempt from paying.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Portugal?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Portugal and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS starts, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Portugal Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The general Schengen short-stay visa fee is €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries.

faq.question: What income do I need for Portugal's residency visa for people living from passive income?
faq.answer: For passive income, Portugal's visa portal asks for a document certifying revenue from movable and immovable property, intellectual or financial assets, and it bases means of subsistence on the minimum monthly salary: 920€ in 2026 for the first adult. The national visa fee is €110, and the Foreigners Act says the residence visa allows its holder to enter Portugal in order to apply for a residence permit.

faq.question: Does Portugal have a digital nomad visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Portugal's visa portal lists a residency visa for the exercise of a professional activity done remotely (digital nomads). It asks for proof of average monthly income for the last three months with a minimum value equivalent to four monthly minimum guaranteed remunerations. The national visa fee is €110.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Portugal without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens do not need a visa.
